\textbf{The error is set by the noise gain \(1 + R_f/|Z|\) at the frequency
being measured, not by the electrode's chemistry.} Gain-ranged to the lowest
code in compliance and with no calibration applied, the channel holds
\SI{0.44}{\percent} of magnitude and \SI{1.04}{\degree} of phase from
\SI{0.01}{\hertz} to \SI{20}{\kilo\hertz} on all five loads,
\SI{0.33}{\percent} and \SI{0.29}{\degree} at and below \SI{5}{\kilo\hertz}, and
\SI{0.030}{\percent} and \SI{0.010}{\degree} at and below \SI{1}{\hertz};
ranging badly costs an order of magnitude. Across the corner set the error spans
a factor of two, worst at \SI{85}{\celsius} on every load and gain code, while
phase moves far less, because this corner set does not move the poles. The
320-tap ladder covers \SI{236}{\ohm} to \SI{14.79}{\mega\ohm}, \num{4.80}
decades, each gain code spanning \num{2.81} of them between the
\(\pm\SI{0.80}{\volt}\) output compliance and one converter code of output
fundamental; adjacent codes overlap by more than a decade, so there are no
impedance seams. The usable band is \SI{0.1}{\hertz} to \SI{5.3}{\kilo\hertz},
set by a \(\pm\SI{0.573}{\degree}\) phase gate and not by magnitude. The
feedback pole sets that gate, so it is a poly and capacitor quantity: cornered
as well, it falls to \SI{2.5}{\kilo\hertz} on a worst-case die.

\paragraph{Measured through the converter.} An \SI{11.000}{\kilo\ohm} load at
gain code 20, excited by the real reference ladder and read through the input
multiplexer and an extracted converter, demodulates from \num{256} converter
codes to \(+0.343\,\%\) of magnitude and \SI{-2.94}{\degree} of phase against
the small-signal analysis of the same load and gain code
(Figure~\ref{fig:eis-codelevel}). Three demodulations of that one record
attribute the magnitude error completely, and \textbf{the converter's whole cost
is one number}: a \(+0.636\,\%\) inter-channel gain mismatch, which two points
of gain calibration remove. The phase term is the sampling grid and not the
converter --- one converter serving two channels samples them half a conversion
apart, which costs \(180\,f/f_s\) on a two-level excitation --- so it is
deterministic and needs no calibration; uncorrected, the
\(\pm\SI{0.573}{\degree}\) gate caps an interleaved read at
\SI{2.77}{\kilo\hertz}. One record, one die, one frequency, one resistive load:
a deterministic attribution, not a distribution.

\input{include/analog/fig_eis_codelevel.tex}

\paragraph{Across a wafer the spread is the feedback resistance.} At the bottom
gain code and the nominal corner, \num{500} samples give
\(\sigma = \SI{10.91}{\percent}\) with process variation alone and
\SI{0.43}{\percent} with mismatch alone, against \SI{11.12}{\percent} with both
over \num{654}. \textbf{A stored nominal resistance law is
therefore unusable as a calibration constant}: it puts that whole spread on the
answer, \(\sigma = \SI{10.2}{\percent}\) of magnitude, the bottom-code run's own
\num{649} dies reading \(-32.1\,\%\) to \(+30.6\,\%\) below the feedback pole,
on top of the \SI{9}{\percent} nominal offset the law already carries at that
code. \textbf{One dc measurement of the feedback resistance per chip removes
essentially all of it}: \(\sigma = \SI{0.0006}{\percent}\)
(Figure~\ref{fig:eis-mccal}). Phase escapes the argument --- the feedback
resistance is a real scale factor, so a chip with no gain calibration at all
still reports phase to the accuracy above. Above the feedback pole a dc
calibration cannot help and only a ratio against a known impedance measured at
the same frequency does: on the fresh electrode at gain code 63 and
\SI{5}{\kilo\hertz} a stored dc resistance gives
\(6.85 \pm \SI{1.88}{\percent}\) against the ratio's
\(2.51 \pm \SI{0.83}{\percent}\). \textbf{That calibration impedance must be
switchable across decades}: matched to the load it reaches
\(\sigma = \SI{0.0002}{\percent}\); against a standard \num{9.2} times away in
magnitude it injects \SI{0.18}{\percent}, \num{300} times worse than the dc
calibration it replaces.

\input{include/analog/fig_eis_mccal.tex}
